articles.title: How Argentina’s battery-powered Tren Solar is recharging an ancient Andean route
articles.summary:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM There are places where the land itself seems to generate energy. The Quebrada de Humahuaca in Jujuy province, in Argentina’s far northwest, is one of them. At altitude, in clear desert air, the valley gets solar radiation that would be hard to match anywhere at lower elevation. For most […]
The post How Argentina’s battery-powered Tren Solar is recharging an ancient Andean route first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News.
articles.content:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM

There are places where the land itself seems to generate energy. The Quebrada de Humahuaca in Jujuy province, in Argentina’s far northwest, is one of them. At altitude, in clear desert air, the valley gets solar radiation that would be hard to match anywhere at lower elevation. For most of its history, that energy was just weather. Now it runs a train.

The Tren Solar de la Quebrada, Latin America’s first solar-powered railway, has been running since June 2024, carrying passengers 42 kilometers (26 miles) through the Andes between six towns. The route passes through a UNESCO World Heritage valley that people have crossed for thousands of years.

A route through the Andes for millennia

The Quebrada de Humahuaca is not a valley that has been waiting for discovery. Pre-Inca peoples used it as a trading route. Spanish colonial roads followed the same path centuries later. Today, it connects communities between Volcán in the south and Tilcara in the north, places that had passenger rail for much of the 20th century, and then didn’t.

Rail disappeared from the valley around 30 years ago. The Tren Solar brought it back, minus the diesel.

How the battery system works without a grid

Six batteries and two fast-charging stops

The train does not generate electricity from panels on its roof. Rather, the two-car train runs on six lithium batteries, charged with solar energy from Jujuy province. That gives it a range of 100 to 120 kilometers (62 to 75 miles), more than twice its current route length. Fast-charging stations at Volcán and Purmamarca allow top-ups along the way; a third is planned for the northern terminus at Tilcara.

Regenerative braking in the mountains

Mountain railways brake often. The Tren Solar captures some of that motion and stores it as electricity. No diesel, no overhead lines: on a route where neither exists anyway, that’s the whole point.

Thirty years without rail, now 90,000 riders

More than 90,000 people have taken the train since its June 2024 launch, according to the Jujuy government. Tourism was part of the intent, but the train also matters to people who live in the valley. The communities here are strung along a narrow corridor with no real alternative to road travel.

Where a system like this makes sense

The Tren Solar works partly because Jujuy has no energy shortage. Solar conditions here are among the best in the world, and the train’s battery range covers more than twice its current route. Standard electric rail needs overhead lines and a grid connection. There isn’t one here, so the design simply went around it.

The same problem shows up elsewhere. In Switzerland in 2025, a startup called Sun-Ways put 48 solar panels between the rails on a 100-meter (328-foot) test track, generating around 16,000 kilowatt-hours in its first year. The company has since signed an agreement to try the system in Italy. The underlying issue is the same in both cases: much of the world’s rail still runs on diesel, and the electrical grids that could replace it don’t reach everywhere. For those places, the resource is often already there. It just hasn’t had a train built around it yet.

articles.title: Ocean heatwaves are hiding months of extra warming
articles.summary: Marine heatwaves may be only the most intense part of much longer warming events, with elevated temperatures sometimes lingering for months. Researchers found that conventional measurements underestimate total heat exposure by more than 150% on average, potentially overlooking a major source of stress on marine ecosystems.
articles.content:
Anyone who has ever heated a pot of water knows that temperature depends on more than how hot something gets. Time matters too. Yet marine heatwaves (MHWs) have traditionally been studied as distinct events with clearly defined beginnings and endings.

New research led by William & Mary's VIMS & Batten School suggests that approach may overlook a major part of the heat marine ecosystems actually experience. The researchers developed a framework for measuring cumulative exposure not only during MHWs, but also during the extended periods of unusually warm water that can occur before and after them.

Marine heatwaves are part of longer warming periods

The study, published in Nature's Communications Earth & Environment, categorizes warming periods that occur ahead of and following MHWs. Using long term observations from 20 U.S. estuaries, the researchers developed a way to measure total heat exposure by viewing marine heatwaves as part of broader warming episodes rather than as isolated events.

"We started to notice these warm-water anomalies on either side of marine heatwaves and realized that they're actually embedded within larger periods of warm water," explained lead author Ricardo Utzig Nardi M.S. '25, a research specialist working with coauthor Piero Mazzini, assistant professor at VIMS & the Batten School of Coastal & Marine Sciences. "It sounds obvious, but studies usually focus only on the marine heatwave window and that's not an accurate representation of real-world conditions."

Nardi found that these broader stretches of unusually warm water can continue for weeks or even months, with the marine heatwave occurring somewhere within that longer period. In many cases, the warming before and after the MHW contributed as much or even more cumulative heat exposure than the heatwave itself.

"We can no longer look at marine heatwaves in isolation when assessing the impact of warming events on coastal and oceanic ecosystems," said Mazzini. "We must acknowledge the larger framework in which they exist and this research provides a way to do just that."

Decades of data reveal underestimated heat stress

The researchers examined more than 2,580 MHWs recorded across 20 U.S. estuaries over two decades. Their analysis found that conventional assessments underestimate total heat exposure by more than 150% on average, a difference that could have important consequences for understanding ecosystem health.

"Consider spending time in the sun," said Nardi, explaining the importance of cumulative heat exposure. "Your risk of sunburn depends on both sunlight intensity and how long you're exposed to it. A few minutes may cause little harm, but hours of exposure can take a toll. It's similar for marine organisms and warm water. Their biological responses depend not only on how warm the water becomes, but also on how long that warming persists. Prolonged, cumulative heat exposure, especially when combined with other stressors, can create conditions that some species may not be able to survive."

The results indicate that warm water anomalies occurring before and after a heatwave are largely independent of the MHW itself. That finding challenges the usual way scientists interpret thermal stress and provides a new approach for estimating total heat exposure across coastal ecosystems.

Two types of marine heatwaves emerge

The researchers also separated MHWs into two broad categories. About two thirds were classified as "individual" events. These occurred within approximately 60 days of elevated temperatures extending beyond the MHW itself.

The remaining one third were classified as "compound" events. These were associated with much longer periods of warming (approximately 90 days) before and after MHWs and generated more than three times the cumulative heat exposure produced by the MHW itself.

"As you can see, these are remarkably long periods of thermal exposure," explained Mazzini. "Many laboratory experiments simulate marine heatwaves by increasing temperatures for a few days or weeks in total. Our findings demonstrate that while these experiments hold value, they often fail to capture the prolonged thermal exposure organisms experience in nature. Our research provides a new framework for designing experiments that reflect natural marine heatwave conditions and quantify cumulative heat exposure, allowing scientists to better evaluate the biological impacts of marine heatwaves across ecosystems."

Rethinking how marine heatwaves are studied

The work adds to a growing body of MHW research from faculty and researchers at VIMS & Batten School. Mazzini and Nathan Shunk, a third-year Ph.D. student, recently published a study defining "vertical marine heatwaves" and developing a classification system for them in the Bay.

Last year, Nardi and Mazzini also published research forecasting an increase in MHWs along the U.S. East Coast. That work identified connections between marine heatwaves and large scale climate patterns, including El Niño and the Pacific Decadal Oscillation.

"This study is an example of outstanding science born from a simple question about temperature's relationship to water quality conditions in estuaries," said Mazzini. "It was made possible by NOAA's National Estuarine Research Reserve System and its long-term, high-frequency temperature observations. Comprehensive monitoring programs like these allow us to ask bigger questions and uncover patterns that would otherwise remain hidden."

Longer warming could intensify ecosystem stress

The findings could also help coastal communities and resource managers better understand how prolonged warming affects marine environments. Long periods of elevated water temperatures can intensify other environmental pressures, including low oxygen conditions and harmful algal blooms.

Together, these stresses can place additional pressure on ecosystems ranging from seagrass beds to coral reefs. Including warming periods before and after MHWs in ecological assessments and laboratory experiments could help researchers create more realistic estimates of ecosystem vulnerability and provide better information for conservation and management decisions.

"This research has the potential to shift our understanding of the role warming waters play in ecosystem health by widening our focus beyond the heatwave window, so that we consider the full impact of temperature across time," explained Nardi. "I'm excited to discover what we may have missed before with this new perspective."

As MHWs become more frequent and intense, measuring their full cumulative impact may become increasingly important for protecting coastal resources and helping communities prepare for future environmental change.

articles.personality_title: New research shows marine heatwaves last longer and cause more warming than thought
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Marine heatwaves are periods when ocean temperatures rise much higher than usual. Scientists have studied these heatwaves as single events, focusing only on the hottest days.

**What happened** – Researchers from William & Mary’s VIMS and Batten School discovered that marine heatwaves are part of longer warming periods. By studying 20 U.S. estuaries over 20 years, they found that ocean water stays warmer for weeks or months before and after the heatwaves. This longer warming raises the total heat exposure by over 150% compared to past measurements.

**Impact** – This finding changes how we understand heat stress on ocean life. Marine animals and plants don’t just feel the heat during the peak heatwave, but also during the longer warm periods around it. This extra heat can harm ecosystems more than scientists realized. The study also identified two types of heatwaves: shorter "individual" events and longer "compound" events, with the latter causing much more heat stress.

**What's next step** – Scientists plan to use this new way of measuring heat exposure to improve experiments and better predict how marine life will respond to warming oceans. Coastal managers can also use this knowledge to protect ecosystems by considering the full length of warming, not just the heatwave days.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Marine heatwaves last longer and cause more total warming than previously known, changing how we measure and respond to ocean heat stress.
articles.personality_title_fr: Une nouvelle étude révèle que les vagues de chaleur marine durent plus longtemps et réchauffent davantage que prévu
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Les vagues de chaleur marine sont des périodes où la température de l’océan augmente beaucoup plus que d’habitude. Jusqu’à présent, les scientifiques les étudiaient comme des événements isolés, en se concentrant sur les jours les plus chauds.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Des chercheurs de William & Mary, VIMS et Batten School ont découvert que les vagues de chaleur marine font partie de périodes de réchauffement plus longues. En étudiant 20 estuaires américains sur 20 ans, ils ont trouvé que l’eau restait chaude pendant des semaines ou des mois avant et après ces vagues. Cela augmente l’exposition totale à la chaleur de plus de 150 % par rapport aux mesures passées.

**Impact** – Cette découverte change notre compréhension du stress thermique sur la vie marine. Les animaux et plantes marins ressentent la chaleur non seulement pendant la vague, mais aussi pendant toute la période de réchauffement prolongée. Cette chaleur supplémentaire peut endommager les écosystèmes plus que prévu. L’étude a aussi identifié deux types de vagues : des événements plus courts "individuels" et des événements plus longs "composés", ces derniers causant beaucoup plus de stress thermique.

**Prochaines étapes** – Les scientifiques vont utiliser cette nouvelle méthode pour mieux concevoir leurs expériences et prévoir comment la vie marine réagira aux océans qui se réchauffent. Les gestionnaires côtiers pourront mieux protéger les écosystèmes en tenant compte de toute la durée du réchauffement, pas seulement des jours de vague de chaleur.

**Conclusion en une phrase** – Les vagues de chaleur marine durent plus longtemps et causent un réchauffement total plus important que ce que l’on pensait, ce qui change la manière de mesurer et de gérer le stress thermique océanique.
articles.personality_title_es: Nueva investigación muestra que las olas de calor marinas duran más y causan más calentamiento de lo pensado
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Las olas de calor marinas son periodos en los que la temperatura del océano sube mucho más de lo normal. Los científicos las han estudiado como eventos separados, enfocándose solo en los días más calientes.

**Qué pasó** – Investigadores de William & Mary, VIMS y Batten School descubrieron que las olas de calor marinas forman parte de periodos de calentamiento más largos. Al estudiar 20 estuarios en EE.UU. durante 20 años, encontraron que el agua permanece caliente semanas o meses antes y después de las olas de calor. Esto aumenta la exposición total al calor en más del 150% comparado con mediciones anteriores.

**Impacto** – Este hallazgo cambia cómo entendemos el estrés por calor en la vida marina. Los animales y plantas marinas sienten el calor no solo durante la ola de calor, sino también durante todo el periodo prolongado de calentamiento. Este calor extra puede dañar los ecosistemas más de lo que se creía. El estudio también identificó dos tipos de olas: eventos más cortos "individuales" y eventos más largos "compuestos", siendo estos últimos los que causan mucho más estrés térmico.

**Próximos pasos** – Los científicos usarán esta nueva forma de medir la exposición al calor para mejorar los experimentos y predecir mejor cómo responderá la vida marina al calentamiento oceánico. Los gestores costeros podrán proteger mejor los ecosistemas considerando todo el tiempo de calentamiento, no solo los días de la ola de calor.

**Conclusión en una frase** – Las olas de calor marinas duran más y causan un calentamiento total mayor del que se pensaba, cambiando cómo medimos y respondemos al estrés térmico en los océanos.

articles.title: How did Earth get its water? Inside the extreme machine seeking answers
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 30 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02978-4The Z machine in New Mexico generates shockwaves that can simulate conditions deep inside our planet.
articles.content:
Geoscientists have been debating whether Earth (right) trapped water in its interior during its formation some 4.5 billion years ago.Credit: SPL/Alamy

Albuquerque, New Mexico

The Z machine at Sandia National Laboratories is an extreme device. Its ring of capacitors fill a room about the size of two basketball courts. When they fire, they unleash an electrical pulse that, for a few billionths of a second, delivers more power than is generated by all the world’s power plants at any given moment. This pulse triggers a shockwave that subjects anything at the machine’s centre to pressures equivalent to those found deep inside giant gas planets and nuclear explosions.

Earth’s oldest crystals suggest an early start for plate tectonics

Late last month, Alisha Clark, a mineral physicist at the University of Colorado in Boulder, harnessed the power of the Z machine to study something closer to home: Earth’s interior. Nature joined her to observe the final ‘shot’ taken with the machine in a multi-year project to better understand the origins of water on Earth.

This focus on Earth is unusual for the Z machine. Located on the Kirtland Air Force Base in Albuquerque, New Mexico, the device was originally built for testing materials to guarantee the reliability of the US stockpile of nuclear weapons without having to detonate bombs. That’s still mostly what it’s used for. But about 10% of the shots taken with the device each year are set aside for fundamental research.

Firing the machine requires months of preparation and input from more than a hundred people. Each shot takes a full day to set up and costs around US$250,000. As a result, few requests to use the machine are approved for researchers studying planets, and even fewer for people investigating Earth.

Mineral physicist Alisha Clark examines a target containing water-infused glass samples before it is loaded into the Z machine.Credit: James Dinneen/Nature

But the Z machine is crucial for Clark’s work. She suggests that during the early, chaotic days of Earth’s formation, melted rock inside the planet trapped and held onto water — counter to the origin story that geoscientists usually tell. “Earth is a sponge,” she told Nature.

To test this idea, Clark needed to simulate how melted rock behaves under the conditions near Earth’s core as it formed. And that’s where the Z machine came in.

Magma ocean

Around 4.5 billion years ago, Earth — freshly formed from cosmic dust and gas — would have been completely molten, heated by radioactive elements and collisions with other planetary debris, geoscientists say. Given these conditions, one long-standing theory about Earth suggests that any water molecules accumulated inside the planet would have steamed or been blasted off into space and lost. If this were true, all of the water on the planet’s surface today would have been delivered later, by icy comets and asteroids, after the crust cooled. And any water currently in the interior would have been carried there by tectonic plates sinking down into Earth’s mantle.

But there is an alternative possibility. Early Earth, in its molten form, might have held on to some of the original water molecules that it had accumulated from cosmic dust and gas. If this were true, much of the water on Earth’s surface today might have been released from its hot interior through volcanoes over geological time. And even greater volumes — oceans’ worth of water — might have remained in the planet’s interior.

Diamond delivers long-sought mineral from the deep Earth

This idea was inspired by a number of geophysical and geochemical discoveries from the past decade or so that have pointed to a larger reservoir of water in Earth’s interior than could have been delivered by plate tectonics alone. For instance, in 2014, scientists analysed1 a diamond that came from deep in Earth’s mantle. They found that it had a mineral impurity that contained a surprising amount of water dissolved inside its crystal structure.

But researchers have struggled to explain how so much water could have stayed trapped inside a molten Earth. Clark’s work on the Z machine puts forward one idea from a pool of possibilities2 that scientists are considering.

She has been using the machine to test how the presence of water affects the compressibility of molten glass — a proxy for melted silicate rock — under extreme pressures. This involves sending a shockwave through glass samples infused with water to briefly recreate the conditions that occur near Earth’s centre.

In experiments that she had run previously, she found that the glass, when infused with a lot of water, seems to become stiffer, but as pressure increases, it becomes easier to compress. “It becomes more squishy the more you squish it, which is not normal behaviour,” she says. This, she thinks, could mean that melted rock is good at trapping water under the pressures found inside Earth’s mantle, suggesting a way that the planet could have held onto water even during its molten ‘magma ocean’ phase.
articles.reasoning: The article reports on a significant scientific breakthrough using the Z machine to simulate Earth's interior conditions, providing new insights into the origin and retention of Earth's water. This research has broad implications for understanding Earth's formation and water cycle, benefiting the general public's knowledge of planetary science and environmental history. The story is focused, detailed, and highlights a meaningful advancement in geoscience.
articles.personality_title: New experiments reveal how early Earth may have kept its water
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Scientists have long wondered how Earth got its water. One idea is that water arrived later, carried by comets and asteroids after the planet cooled. Another is that Earth trapped water inside when it was still molten, about 4.5 billion years ago.

**What happened** – At Sandia National Laboratories in New Mexico, researchers used a powerful device called the Z machine to recreate the extreme pressures inside early Earth. Mineral physicist Alisha Clark tested how water mixed with melted rock behaves under these conditions. The machine sends shockwaves through water-infused glass to simulate the planet’s deep interior.

This challenges the old idea that all early water was lost and suggests much of Earth's water might have come from inside, released later by volcanoes.

**What's next step** – Scientists will continue using the Z machine and other tools to better understand how water stayed inside Earth and how it shaped the planet’s development. This research could help explain not only Earth’s history but also water on other planets.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Powerful lab experiments suggest early Earth held onto water inside its molten interior, changing how we think about the planet’s water origins.
articles.personality_title_fr: De nouvelles expériences montrent comment la Terre primitive a pu conserver son eau
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Les scientifiques se demandent depuis longtemps comment la Terre a obtenu son eau. Une idée est que l'eau est arrivée plus tard, transportée par des comètes et des astéroïdes après que la planète s’est refroidie. Une autre est que la Terre a piégé l'eau à l'intérieur quand elle était encore en fusion, il y a environ 4,5 milliards d'années.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Au Laboratoire national Sandia au Nouveau-Mexique, des chercheurs ont utilisé un appareil puissant appelé la machine Z pour recréer les pressions extrêmes à l'intérieur de la Terre primitive. La physicienne des minéraux Alisha Clark a testé comment l'eau mélangée à de la roche fondue se comporte dans ces conditions. La machine envoie des ondes de choc à travers du verre infusé d'eau pour simuler l'intérieur profond de la planète.

**Impact** – Les expériences de Clark montrent que la roche fondue contenant de l'eau devient plus facile à comprimer sous pression, ce qui signifie qu'elle pourrait retenir l'eau à l'intérieur du manteau terrestre même lorsque la planète était une boule chaude et en fusion. Cela remet en question l’ancienne idée que toute l’eau primitive a été perdue et suggère qu’une grande partie de l’eau de la Terre vient de l’intérieur, libérée plus tard par les volcans.

**Prochaines étapes** – Les scientifiques vont continuer à utiliser la machine Z et d’autres outils pour mieux comprendre comment l’eau est restée à l’intérieur de la Terre et comment elle a influencé le développement de la planète. Cette recherche pourrait aussi aider à expliquer la présence d’eau sur d’autres planètes.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Des expériences en laboratoire puissantes suggèrent que la Terre primitive a conservé de l’eau dans son intérieur en fusion, changeant notre compréhension de l’origine de l’eau sur la planète.
articles.personality_title_es: Nuevos experimentos revelan cómo la Tierra primitiva pudo conservar su agua
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Los científicos han preguntado por mucho tiempo cómo obtuvo agua la Tierra. Una idea es que el agua llegó después, traída por cometas y asteroides cuando el planeta se enfrió. Otra idea es que la Tierra atrapó agua en su interior cuando aún estaba derretida, hace unos 4.5 mil millones de años.

**Qué pasó** – En el Laboratorio Nacional Sandia en Nuevo México, investigadores usaron un dispositivo poderoso llamado máquina Z para recrear las presiones extremas dentro de la Tierra primitiva. La física mineral Alisha Clark probó cómo se comporta el agua mezclada con roca derretida bajo estas condiciones. La máquina envía ondas de choque a través de vidrio con agua para simular el interior profundo del planeta.

**Impacto** – Los experimentos de Clark muestran que la roca derretida con agua se vuelve más fácil de comprimir bajo presión, lo que significa que podría atrapar agua dentro del manto terrestre, incluso cuando la Tierra era una bola caliente y derretida. Esto desafía la idea antigua de que toda el agua temprana se perdió y sugiere que gran parte del agua de la Tierra vino de su interior y fue liberada más tarde por volcanes.

**Próximo paso** – Los científicos seguirán usando la máquina Z y otras herramientas para entender mejor cómo el agua permaneció dentro de la Tierra y cómo esto afectó el desarrollo del planeta. Esta investigación también podría ayudar a explicar el agua en otros planetas.

**Resumen en una frase** – Experimentos de laboratorio poderosos sugieren que la Tierra primitiva mantuvo agua en su interior derretido, cambiando cómo entendemos el origen del agua del planeta.

articles.title: In Brazil’s capital, residents grow their own heat-fighting solutions
articles.summary: Life in the favelas surrounding Brazil’s capital brings the health risks of extreme heat — a symptom of the global inequities of green space access
articles.content:
This story by Lobato Felizola was originally published on Dialogue Earth’s website on July 14, 2026. It is republished here under a partnership agreement with Global Voices, with edits. It’s also part of Dialogue Earth’s work on the Community Adaptations to City Heat (CATCH) project, in partnership with Boston University.

Brasília was designed to be a green city. Tree planting was so central to planning for the Brazilian capital that it was described as a park city. This is evident in its central area, with cool, tree-lined avenues and green parks where locals enjoy walks. The city was built in just 41 months, replacing the savanna-type biome Cerrado with a gleaming new capital.

But 30 kilometers (19 miles) away from the Plano Piloto, in the Sol Nascente favela, the central area designed as an airplane, this ecosystem was replaced with concrete. While the Plano Piloto averages 138 sq meters (1,485 sq feet) of green space per inhabitant, a University of Brasília (UnB) study of urban green spaces finds that in some peripheral areas of Brasília, that figure can be up to 23 times smaller. These outlying areas are characterised by “limited vegetation and greater distances to green spaces,” says the study.

Sol Nascente consists of mostly tarmac-surfaced streets, with houses crammed on top of one another and narrow pavements that can barely accommodate pedestrians, let alone trees. Heat is a huge problem. “There are times when the whole street is in the sun, and the air doesn’t circulate,” says resident Francisco Silva.

The health impacts can be severe. “Everything gets very dry, and my nose bleeds,” says the 34-year-old. Silva suffers from rhinitis and bronchitis that disrupt his sleep. “If I close the window, I can’t breathe; if I open it, dry wind and dust come in.”

During the dry season, he washes the yard every day, spreads wet towels around the house, and wears a mask. To beat the heat, Silva is renovating his house to make way for grass and saplings. On the pavement, he planted the only tree on the street – a solitary ipe, a common species in Latin America.

Valdir Steinke, who authored the University of Brasília study, says Brazil’s Federal District (where Brasília is located) reflects a national pattern of “green spaces concentrated in the most affluent areas, whilst the outskirts have almost none.” Indeed, the average per capita household income in Plano Piloto is 12 times higher than in Sol Nascente. “It is a stark and unvarnished portrait of a socio-economic segregation pattern in which urban planning in the outskirts ignores nature,” says Steinke.

These problems are being exacerbated as climate change drives up temperatures, increasing mortality and morbidity. In response, the local government is planning a tree planting program, and residents are turning to “guerrilla gardening” where urban planning has failed.

Green inequality is a global challenge

Sol Nascente emerged in the 1990s on illegally occupied rural land. Today, more than 70,000 people live in the 9-sq-kilometre (3.4-sq-mile) territory. This population density is almost 16 times higher than the Federal District average. With its tarmac, sparse vegetation and high concentration of residents, the favela provides ideal conditions for a so-called urban heat island.

“Concrete and tarmac absorb and retain the sun’s heat more efficiently than vegetation, whilst trees provide cooling through shade and humidity,” explains Gregory Wellenius, director of the Center for Climate and Health at Boston University in the US.

What has happened in Sol Nascente follows a global pattern. A recent analysis of 199 cities around the world concluded that inequality in access to green spaces is widespread, and the level of disparity in cities in the Global South is twice that of the North.

“Extreme heat maps look very similar to maps of low-income neighbourhoods,” Jeremy Hoffman, a researcher at Groundwork USA, a network of American organisations working for climate justice. “Heat hotspots tend to overlap with areas characterised by higher poverty, lower educational attainment, higher rates of chronic disease and less access to green spaces.”

3-30-300

Cecil Konijnendijk, an expert in urban forests and an honorary professor at the University of British Columbia in Canada, proposed the “3-30-300” rule to tackle green inequality in cities. The rule stipulates that every person should be able to see at least three trees from their window, live in a neighbourhood with at least 30 percent tree coverage, and be no more than 300 metres (984 feet) away from a park or green space to ensure visual and physical access to nature and its benefits.

The rule has been adopted by urban planners around the world. It already guides tree planting policies in Belgium, Sweden, the Netherlands, the US and Canada.

In Brazil, the National Urban Tree Planting Plan, launched at the UN’s COP30 climate conference in 2025, draws inspiration from this rule. It acknowledges that Brazil’s haphazard urbanisation has led to landscape fragmentation, deforestation and concrete-sealed soil which, combined with climate change, negatively impact urban life.

To reverse this situation, the plan sets targets to be reached by 2045. One is to increase the proportion of residents with at least three trees in their immediate surroundings, which would provide green space access to around 40 million additional people.

Some experts question how universally useful the 3-30-300 rule is. Paulina Achurra, from the educational platform Arq.Futuro, warns that greening programmes cannot help in communities with “barely even a pavement on which to plant a tree.”

According to Achurra, speaking during an event in São Paulo, “although there is a lack of innovative solutions that incorporate green spaces, they must be feasible to implement in our cities [in the Global South].”

Extreme heat brings extreme risk

Larissa Brenda Cordeiro, who chairs the Daughters of the Earth Institute (IFT), a socio-environmental justice organisation in Sol Nascente, says the afternoon heat can make it impossible for the organisation to carry out meetings or work in its office. With her asthma and fibromyalgia, she also feels the physical effects: muscle and joint pain. “I feel really unwell in both the cold and during periods of extreme heat.”

Patricia Fabian, a heat expert at Boston University, says people living in urban heat islands are more exposed to the harmful effects of high temperatures: “The hotter the environment, the greater the risk of health impacts, including cardiovascular disease, cognitive problems, respiratory symptoms and even death.”

During the dry season, the temperature in some parts of central Brasília can climb to 37.8ºC (100ºF), while Ceilândia, which incorporated Sol Nascente until 2019, reaches 46.6ºC (116ºF).

Protecting and growing

One of the few green spaces in Sol Nascente is a remnant of Lagoinha Park, which was gradually deforested by encroaching settlements. Buriti palm trees indicate abundant groundwater, but rubbish accumulates haphazardly, including in the springs that feed the Melchior River and the Descoberto Basin, which provide more than 60 percent of the Federal District’s water supply.

In December 2025, the Federal District approved its own plan to reduce the “green deficit” in its outlying areas. In Sol Nascente, the government told Dialogue Earth that planting cannot start until problems such as narrow pavements and a lack of stormwater drainage are fixed, because the saplings would not survive. They did not specify if or when these works would take place.

Today, Lagoinha Park is like a large lawn with few native trees. Activists like Cordeiro hope it can someday become a wooded area with picnic tables and sports courts: “Our dream is for Lagoinha to become a proper park that the public can enjoy.”

They have a role model for such a project: on the border between Sol Nascente and Ceilândia, a conservation project dubbed Floresta da Nasaré grew out of a rubbish tip. In 2009, housewife Nasaré Francisca da Silva took it upon herself to clear a football pitch-sized plot of public land opposite her home. Next, she planted a seedling. “People used to dump all sorts of things there, from building rubble to dead animals,” she recalls. “I’d look at it from my front door, and it made me sad.”

From a seedling grew the agroforest now maintained by neighbours, NGOs and University of Brasília researchers. Da Silva’s care for the land was formalised in 2023 by the Federal District’s government. Although it does not receive public investment, there is less risk of land seizure or their work being interrupted without warning.

On hot days, it is still cool beneath the tree canopy. “Everyone is welcome to come here and cool off from the heat,” says da Silva.

The story provides detailed context about the problem's scale, health impacts, and ongoing solutions, including a large-scale national plan inspired by an internationally recognized rule (3-30-300). This represents meaningful progress in climate adaptation, urban planning equity, and public health.
articles.personality_title: Residents and officials in Brazil’s capital work together to cool their hottest neighborhoods
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Brasília, Brazil’s capital, was planned as a green city with many trees and parks. But in poorer neighborhoods far from the center, like the Sol Nascente favela, there are very few green spaces. These areas have lots of concrete and very little vegetation, causing extreme heat that affects people’s health.

**What happened** – Residents of Sol Nascente are planting trees and grass to cool their streets and homes. The government is planning a large tree-planting program to bring more green spaces to these hot neighborhoods. This follows a national plan inspired by the “3-30-300” rule, which says everyone should see at least three trees from their window, live in a place with 30% tree coverage, and be close to a park.

**Impact** – This effort helps reduce heat in crowded, poor areas where temperatures can be dangerously high. Trees provide shade and cool the air, improving health and comfort for thousands of people. The community’s work, like turning a former rubbish dump into a green forest, shows how local action can create lasting change even where city planning has failed.

**What's next step** – The local government needs to fix problems like narrow sidewalks and poor drainage before planting more trees. Meanwhile, residents and activists continue greening their neighborhoods and hope to expand parks and green areas. These combined efforts aim to make Brasília’s outskirts cooler and healthier by 2045.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Community action and government plans are joining to bring more trees and cooler spaces to Brazil’s hottest, most crowded neighborhoods, improving health and quality of life.
articles.personality_title_fr: À Brasilia, habitants et autorités unissent leurs forces pour rafraîchir les quartiers les plus chauds
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Brasilia, la capitale du Brésil, a été conçue comme une ville verte avec de nombreux arbres et parcs. Mais dans les quartiers pauvres éloignés du centre, comme la favela Sol Nascente, il y a très peu d’espaces verts. Ces zones sont couvertes de béton et ont peu de végétation, ce qui provoque une chaleur extrême qui nuit à la santé des habitants.

**Ce qui s'est passé** – Les habitants de Sol Nascente plantent des arbres et du gazon pour rafraîchir leurs rues et leurs maisons. Le gouvernement prévoit un grand programme de plantation d’arbres pour créer plus d’espaces verts dans ces quartiers chauds. Cela s’inscrit dans un plan national inspiré de la règle « 3-30-300 », qui recommande que chacun puisse voir au moins trois arbres depuis sa fenêtre, vivre dans un quartier avec 30 % de couverture arborée, et être proche d’un parc.

**Impact** – Ces actions aident à réduire la chaleur dans les zones pauvres et densément peuplées où les températures peuvent être dangereuses. Les arbres offrent de l’ombre et rafraîchissent l’air, améliorant la santé et le confort de milliers de personnes. Le travail des communautés, comme la transformation d’une ancienne décharge en forêt urbaine, montre comment l’action locale peut créer un changement durable même quand la planification urbaine a échoué.

**Prochaine étape** – Le gouvernement local doit d’abord résoudre des problèmes comme les trottoirs étroits et le mauvais drainage avant de planter davantage d’arbres. En attendant, les habitants et les militants continuent de verdir leurs quartiers et espèrent agrandir les parcs. Ces efforts conjoints visent à rendre les périphéries de Brasilia plus fraîches et plus saines d’ici 2045.

**Phrase clé** – L’action communautaire et les plans gouvernementaux s’unissent pour apporter plus d’arbres et d’espaces frais aux quartiers les plus chauds et les plus peuplés du Brésil, améliorant ainsi la santé et la qualité de vie.
articles.personality_title_es: En la capital de Brasil, residentes y autoridades trabajan juntos para enfriar los barrios más calurosos
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Brasilia, la capital de Brasil, fue planeada como una ciudad verde con muchos árboles y parques. Pero en los barrios pobres alejados del centro, como la favela Sol Nascente, hay muy pocos espacios verdes. Estas zonas tienen mucho concreto y poca vegetación, lo que provoca un calor extremo que afecta la salud de las personas.

**Qué pasó** – Los residentes de Sol Nascente están plantando árboles y césped para enfriar sus calles y casas. El gobierno está planificando un gran programa de plantación de árboles para traer más espacios verdes a estos barrios calurosos. Esto sigue un plan nacional inspirado en la regla “3-30-300”, que dice que todos deberían ver al menos tres árboles desde su ventana, vivir en un vecindario con un 30 % de cobertura arbórea y estar cerca de un parque.

**Impacto** – Este esfuerzo ayuda a reducir el calor en áreas pobres y densamente pobladas donde las temperaturas pueden ser peligrosamente altas. Los árboles proporcionan sombra y enfrían el aire, mejorando la salud y el bienestar de miles de personas. El trabajo de la comunidad, como convertir un antiguo basurero en un bosque verde, muestra cómo la acción local puede crear un cambio duradero incluso donde la planificación urbana ha fallado.

**Próximo paso** – El gobierno local necesita arreglar problemas como las aceras estrechas y el mal drenaje antes de plantar más árboles. Mientras tanto, los residentes y activistas continúan embelleciendo sus barrios y esperan ampliar parques y áreas verdes. Estos esfuerzos combinados buscan hacer que las afueras de Brasilia sean más frescas y saludables para 2045.

**Frase clave** – La acción comunitaria y los planes gubernamentales se unen para llevar más árboles y espacios frescos a los barrios más calurosos y densamente poblados de Brasil, mejorando la salud y la calidad de vida.
